headline: Robinson's Hole stacked: albies stacked on peanuts, bonito riding shotgun
subhead: The bait finally tightened against the rocks this week, and the fleet from Woods Hole to Menemsha found out fast.
body_markdown:
The bait told the story this week before a single rod bent. Peanut bunker and silversides that had been scattered loose across Buzzards Bay for the last two weeks finally balled up tight against the rocks at Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole, and where the bait pinches down like that in September, the albies and bonito are never far behind. By midweek the fleet working the Elizabeth Islands rips had their answer — false albacore blitzing on top in short, violent windows, bonito mixed underneath picking off the same peanuts a little deeper in the column.

We flagged this exact setup a week ago — said to expect the bonito/albie action to keep building through the week with striper interest ramping as the new moon tide came in, and that's precisely what showed up. The tide range has widened since, the current through Robinson's and Quick's is running harder on both the flood and the ebb, and that extra push is exactly what's needed to pin bait against structure instead of letting it spread out over open water. Warm surface water sitting on top of a cooling Buzzards Bay base has created a sharp edge right along the rips, and that edge is doing the concentrating work for us.

The best albie windows have been the last two hours of the ebb at Robinson's Hole, when the current funnels bait out of Buzzards Bay and into Vineyard Sound and the fish stack up on the downcurrent side of the rocks. Quick's Hole has been running on a similar clock, maybe twenty minutes behind. Small profile metals — half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks, Albie Snax in bone or pink-white, and 3-inch epoxy jigs in olive-over-white — have all produced, but presentation matters more than the lure right now. These fish are eating peanut bunker roughly two to three inches long, so match that size or get ignored. Cast into the boil, let it sink for a two-count, then work it back on a fast, erratic retrieve with pauses — the pause is when the strikes come. Bonito are mixing in on the same baits but tend to sit a touch deeper and hit on a steadier, less jerky retrieve.

Menemsha has been more of a mixed bag. The bite there has been real but spotty — good for twenty minutes around the top of the tide when bait gets pushed against the jetty, then it goes quiet until the next stage. If you only have a short window at Menemsha, fish the last of the incoming through the first thirty minutes of the high, working the rip line off the north side of the channel entrance.

Striped bass are the story building underneath all of this, and it's starting to look like more than stragglers. Bunker schools that had been holding loose in Buzzards Bay are tightening up as water cools, and bass are shadowing them tight to structure around Cuttyhunk and the west end of the Elizabeths. The pattern right now is early and late — first light and the last hour of light, working live or fresh-dead peanut bunker on a fish-finder rig along the rockpiles off Cuttyhunk's west side, or swimming a bunker spoon through the rip at the mouth of Quick's Hole on the dropping tide. Sizes have been mixed, mostly schoolies and low-slot fish, but the pattern is the one to watch — this is the setup that turns into real numbers of bigger bass as bait keeps evacuating the back bays over the next two to three weeks.

Bluefish have been riding along with the albie schools more than working their own pattern, jumbo blues mixed into the same blitzes at Robinson's Hole and occasionally taking over entirely when the albies move off. Anyone throwing metal into a blitz without wire or a heavier leader has been losing gear — a short length of 40-pound fluorocarbon will cut down on bite-offs without spooking the tuna-family fish.

Fluke fishing has held up as the quieter, reliable piece of the week. The bay-side grounds off Woods Hole and the sandy patches inside Tarpaulin Cove have been giving up keeper fluke to 20 inches on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished slow on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet on the last of the outgoing. Scup have been thick around the same structure, an easy backup bite on small hooks and sandworm strips if the fluke go quiet.

Looking ahead, the setup favors more of the same through the weekend. Wind has been manageable and water color clean along the rips, which is exactly what this bite needs — any real blow out of the southwest would muddy up Robinson's Hole and shut the visual feeding down fast, so keep an eye on the forecast before committing to a long run. If the wind stays cooperative, the albie and bonito window should hold through the coming week, with the bite likely tightening even further as bait gets squeezed by the building tide range into the new moon phase. The bass pattern is the one worth watching hardest — if bunker keep pushing out of the bay at this rate, the next two weeks should bring bigger fish into range at Cuttyhunk and the west end rips, not just the schoolies showing now.
